stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 10, Topic 8.4, Levittown and Suburban Development.
stimulus.text: After the war, builder William Levitt bought farmland outside New York City and built Levittown, a development of thousands of nearly identical, modest houses put up quickly with mass-production methods. The houses were cheap enough for many returning veterans to buy with GI Bill loans. Levitt barred African American buyers with restrictive covenants, and Federal Housing Administration rules encouraged builders to sell only to white buyers. Songwriter Malvina Reynolds mocked the sameness of such developments in 'Little Boxes' (1962).

stem: Levittown best illustrates which reason suburbs grew so fast after the war?

options.text: Builders used mass production while veterans borrowed cheaply to buy houses
Cities paid builders to move families out of urban neighborhoods
options.misconception: Background from the books: builders and veteran loans drove the growth; cities did not pay builders to move families out.

options.text: The federal government banned all new housing inside cities
options.misconception: Background from the books: the government never banned city housing; suburbs grew because houses there were cheap and loans were easy.

options.text: Most Americans left the suburbs to return to farms
options.misconception: Background from the books: the movement ran the other way, from cities to suburbs, not back to farms.

rationales.A: Cheap mass-produced houses plus GI Bill loans put a house within reach of millions of veterans at once.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the growth came from builders and veteran loans, not from cities paying builders to move families.
rationales.C: Background from the books: no law banned new housing in cities; suburbs grew because their houses were cheap and loans were easy.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the postwar movement ran from cities to suburbs, not from suburbs back to farms.
rationales.general:
1. Suburban growth needs two things at once: houses to buy and money to buy them.
2. Background from the books: Levitt's mass production supplied the houses, and GI Bill loans supplied the money.
3. Neither cities paying builders nor a ban on city housing appears in the passage.
Remember: Fast growth usually needs supply and buyers to arrive together.
